title: Phrases and Clauses
summary: Noun phrases, expanded noun phrases, prepositional phrases and fronted adverbials, main and subordinate clauses, and relative clauses: how to spot them, how Checkpoint asks about them, how to use them in your writing, with practice and answers.

blocks.text: Words do not work alone. They join together in groups. Some groups are **phrases** and some are **clauses**. Knowing the difference helps you in two ways. In the **reading** paper, Checkpoint asks you to find the main clause of a sentence, to spot a relative clause, or to explain why a sentence starts with a phrase. In your **writing**, phrases and clauses are the tools you use to build longer, more interesting sentences, which earn Grammar and punctuation marks.

blocks.title: The one rule to remember
blocks.text: A **clause** has a **subject and a verb** (someone or something doing something). A **phrase** does **not** have both. *the old wooden boat* = phrase (no verb). *the boat sank* = clause (subject *the boat* + verb *sank*).
1. Phrase or clause?

rows: after we finished the long journey

blocks.text: Look at *after the long journey* and *after we finished the long journey*. The same first word, but the second one has a subject and a verb, so it is a clause.
2. Noun phrases
A **noun phrase** is a group of words built around **one main noun** (the "head" noun). The other words tell us more about that noun. The whole group works like one noun in the sentence.

items: *the cat* (determiner + noun)
*the grey cat* (determiner + adjective + noun)
***The invaluable advice** came from my grandmother.* Here the whole noun phrase is the subject of the sentence.

blocks.text: To find the head noun, ask: **what is the phrase really about?** In *the tall man in the blue coat*, it is about **the man**.
3. Expanded noun phrases

An **expanded noun phrase** is a noun phrase with **extra describing words** added before and/or after the noun. Writers use them to give the reader a clear picture in very few words. They are one of the best tools in your own writing, especially in stories and descriptions.

rows: Add a prepositional phrase after it
a dark, crumbling castle **on the edge of the cliff**
Or add a relative clause after it
a dark, crumbling castle **that nobody had visited for years**

blocks.title: Do not overdo it
blocks.text: Two adjectives are usually enough: *the cold, grey sea* is strong, but *the cold, grey, wet, huge, dark, noisy sea* is too much. Put a comma between two adjectives of the same kind (*cold, grey*). Choose adjectives that add **new** information or a feeling.

**Why does a writer use an expanded noun phrase?** Possible answers: to give a detailed, clear picture in the reader's mind, to describe the setting or character precisely, to create a mood (for example *the silent, empty corridor* creates a scary mood), or to give a lot of information in a short space (useful in information texts).
4. Prepositional phrases
A **prepositional phrase** starts with a **preposition** and ends with a noun or pronoun: *under the bed*, *after lunch*, *with great care*, *across the busy road*. It has no verb, so it is a phrase.

rows: The book **on the shelf** is mine. (which book?)
She left the room **in a hurry**. (how?) We met **at the station**. (where?) The film starts **after dinner**. (when?)

blocks.text: Writers use prepositional phrases to tell the reader **where**, **when** and **how** things happen, which makes the description precise.
5. Adverbials and fronted adverbials
An **adverbial** is a word, phrase or clause that does the job of an adverb: it tells us **when, where, how, how often** or **why** something happens.

items: one word (an adverb): *Suddenly*, *Yesterday*, *Carefully*
a phrase: *In the morning*, *Without a sound*, *Across the field*, *A few minutes later*
a clause: *As soon as the bell rang*, *When the storm ended*

blocks.text: A **fronted adverbial** is an adverbial that has been moved to the **front** of the sentence, before the subject and verb. It is usually followed by a **comma**.

rows: The crowd cheered **at the end of the race**.
**At the end of the race,** the crowd cheered.
A strange light appeared **without any warning**.
**Without any warning,** a strange light appeared.
We set off for the mountains **early the next morning**.
**Early the next morning,** we set off for the mountains.

blocks.text: **Why does a writer use a fronted adverbial?** Possible answers:

items: to tell the reader **when** or **where** the action happens before it happens, so the scene is set first.
to **link** to the paragraph before and move the story on in time (*Later that day, … / The next morning, …*).
to build **suspense**: the reader waits to find out what happens (*Slowly, very slowly, the door …*).
to make the **manner** stand out (*Without a sound,* puts the focus on the silence).
to **vary sentence openings**, so the writing is not always *He… She… They…*, which makes it more interesting to read.

blocks.title: Fronted adverbials in your own writing
blocks.text: In a story, start three or four sentences with a fronted adverbial of a different kind: one of time (*Just before sunset,*), one of place (*Beneath the old bridge,*), one of manner (*Without a word,*). It varies your openings, links your paragraphs and shows the examiner you control sentence structure.
6. Infinitive phrases
An **infinitive phrase** starts with an infinitive (**to** + verb) and includes the words that go with it: *to finish the project*, *to see the pyramids*, *to win the final match*.

items: As the subject: ***To swim across the lake** was her dream.*
To show purpose (why): *He trained every day **to win the final match**.*

blocks.text: 7. Clauses: main and subordinate
A **clause** has a subject and a verb. There are two kinds.

rows: Can it stand alone as a sentence?
**No.** It needs a main clause to make sense.
with a subordinating conjunction (because, when, although, if…) or a relative pronoun (who, which, that…)

blocks.text: Put them together and you get a **complex sentence**: *We stayed indoors **because it was raining**.* The main clause is *We stayed indoors*; the subordinate clause is *because it was raining*.
**Subordinating conjunctions** that start subordinate clauses:

rows: when, while, as, after, before, until, since, as soon as, whenever
**As soon as the bell rang,** everyone ran outside.
I took a coat **because it looked cold**.
**If you hurry,** you will catch the bus.
**Although she was tired,** she kept running.
He whispered **so that nobody would hear**.

blocks.text: **The subordinate clause can move.** It can come after the main clause or before it. When it comes **first**, put a **comma** after it.

items: *We went home **when the film ended**.*
***When the film ended,** we went home.*

blocks.text: How to find the main clause in four steps

items: Find all the verbs in the sentence.
Find the words that start subordinate clauses (because, when, although, if, who, which, that…). Cover each subordinate clause with your finger.
What is left should make complete sense on its own. That is the main clause.
Copy it **exactly**, every word, and no extra words.

blocks.text: **Worked example:** *Although the path was steep, the hikers who had set off at dawn reached the top before noon.*

items: Cover the subordinate clause *Although the path was steep*.
Cover the relative clause *who had set off at dawn*.
*before noon* is a prepositional phrase, not a clause, so it stays as part of the main clause.
Main clause: **the hikers reached the top before noon**. It makes complete sense alone.

blocks.title: Traps when finding the main clause
items: The main clause is **not always first**. In *When the rain stopped, the children went outside*, the main clause is *the children went outside*.
A relative clause can sit **in the middle** of the main clause: *The dog **that lives next door** barks all night.* Main clause = *The dog barks all night*.
A clause beginning with *because, when, if, although* is **never** the main clause.
Do not copy only part of the main clause. Check that your answer has its subject and its verb.

blocks.text: 8. Relative clauses

A **relative clause** is a kind of subordinate clause that gives **more information about a noun**. It usually comes straight after that noun and begins with a **relative pronoun** (**who, which, that, whose**) or with **where** or **when**.

rows: The girl **who sits next to me** speaks three languages.
Our car, **which is very old**, broke down again.
The cake **that you made** was delicious.
The boy **whose bike was stolen** went to the police.
This is the café **where we first met**.
I remember the day **when we moved to Cairo**.

blocks.text: **Two kinds of relative clause:**

rows: tells us **which one**. Without it, the sentence loses its meaning
The student **who won the prize** is in my class. (which student? the one who won)
adds **extra information** about a noun we already know
My brother, **who loves football**, plays every evening. (we already know who my brother is)

blocks.text: Remember: a **pair of commas** around a relative clause shows **extra information**. If you take the words between the commas away, the sentence still makes sense: *My brother plays every evening.*
**Embedded relative clause:** when the relative clause sits in the **middle** of the main clause, we say it is **embedded**: *The museum, **which opened last year**, has a dinosaur room.*

**Why does a writer use a relative clause?** Possible answers: to give extra information about a person, place or thing without starting a new sentence, to tell the reader exactly which person or thing is meant, to add detail to a description, to join two short sentences into one longer, smoother sentence, or to pack more facts into an information text.

blocks.title: الفرق بين العبارة والجملة وكيف تجد الـ main clause
items: الـ phrase مجموعة كلمات بدون فاعل وفعل معًا، مثل: in the garden.
الـ clause فيها فاعل وفعل، مثل: the children played.
الـ main clause تفهم وحدها كجملة كاملة، أما الـ subordinate clause فتبدأ غالبًا بـ because / when / although / if أو who / which ولا تُفهم وحدها.
لإيجاد الـ main clause: غطِّ كل جزء يبدأ بكلمة ربط أو بـ who / which، والباقي هو الـ main clause، وانسخه كما هو بالضبط.
الـ relative clause بين فاصلتين = معلومة إضافية؛ إذا حذفتها تبقى الجملة صحيحة.

blocks.text: 9. Using phrases and clauses in your writing
Look how one plain sentence grows into a strong one, step by step:

rows: The small, frightened boy ran across the empty playground.
Without looking back, the small, frightened boy ran across the empty playground.
Without looking back, the small, frightened boy ran across the empty playground until he reached the gate.
Without looking back, the small, frightened boy, who had heard the strange noise first, ran across the empty playground until he reached the gate.

blocks.title: Do not make every sentence long
blocks.text: Long sentences full of phrases and clauses are powerful, but a short simple sentence straight after them has a strong effect: *…until he reached the gate. It was locked.* Mix long and short on purpose.
How Checkpoint asks about phrases and clauses

rows: Copy the main clause from this sentence.
Cover the subordinate and relative clauses; copy the rest exactly.
Find who/which/that/whose/where after a noun; underline to the end of the clause.
Tick the sentence that has a subordinate clause.
Look for because, when, although, if, while, until… followed by a subject and verb.
Why does the writer start the sentence with 'Deep in the forest'?
It is a fronted adverbial of place: it sets the scene before the action and creates mood or suspense.
Why does the writer use commas in this sentence?
For example: to separate the subordinate clause at the start from the main clause, or a pair of commas to show extra information in a relative clause.
Find an expanded noun phrase that describes the house.
Copy the determiner, adjectives and noun (plus any phrase after the noun) together, e.g. 'the tall, silent house'.

blocks.text: Practice A: phrase or clause?

items.q: beneath the wooden bridge
items.a: Phrase (prepositional). There is no verb.

items.q: the bridge collapsed
items.a: Clause. Subject 'the bridge' + verb 'collapsed'.

items.q: a basket of ripe mangoes
items.a: Phrase (noun phrase). The head noun is 'basket'.

items.q: while the baby was sleeping
items.a: Clause (subordinate). Subject 'the baby' + verb 'was sleeping', starting with 'while'.

items.q: to protect the turtles
items.a: Phrase (infinitive phrase). No subject.

items.q: which nobody could open
items.a: Clause (relative clause). Subject 'nobody' + verb 'could open'.

blocks.text: Practice B: find the main clause

items.q: When the whistle blew, the players rushed onto the pitch.
items.a: the players rushed onto the pitch

items.q: Our neighbour, who is a doctor, helped the injured cyclist.
items.a: Our neighbour helped the injured cyclist

items.q: We cannot go to the beach unless the wind drops.
items.a: We cannot go to the beach

items.q: Although it was late, the shop that sells sweets was still open.
items.a: the shop was still open

items.q: The parcel arrived after we had left for school.
items.a: The parcel arrived

items.q: Because she practised every day, Hana played the song perfectly at the concert.
items.a: Hana played the song perfectly at the concert

blocks.text: Practice C: relative clauses and expanded noun phrases

items.q: Underline the relative clause: 'The pyramids, which were built thousands of years ago, still amaze visitors.'
items.a: which were built thousands of years ago

items.q: Join with a relative clause: 'I have a friend. Her father is a pilot.'
items.a: I have a friend whose father is a pilot.

items.q: Join with a relative clause: 'We visited the farm. My grandfather grew up there.'
items.a: We visited the farm where my grandfather grew up.

items.q: Is the relative clause essential or extra information? 'The pupils who finished early helped tidy the room.'
items.a: Essential (defining). It tells us which pupils helped — only the ones who finished early — so there are no commas.

items.q: Why are there commas in: 'Mrs Fathy, who teaches music, is retiring this year'?
items.a: The pair of commas shows that 'who teaches music' is extra information about Mrs Fathy. Without it, the sentence still makes sense.

items.q: Expand this noun phrase twice: 'a door'.
items.a: Example: a heavy wooden door (adjectives) → a heavy wooden door at the end of the corridor (+ prepositional phrase).

items.q: What is the head noun in 'the noisy crowd of excited fans'?
items.a: crowd

blocks.text: Practice D: explain the effect (exam style)
Read this short text, then answer the questions.

*Deep beneath the old library, there was a room that nobody remembered. Its walls, which were covered in faded maps, smelt of dust and damp paper. When Ali pushed open the heavy iron door, a cold breath of air rushed past him. He froze.*

items.q: Why does the writer begin the first sentence with 'Deep beneath the old library'? [1]
items.a: It is a fronted adverbial of place. Any one of: it sets the scene before the action / it tells the reader exactly where we are / it creates a mysterious, hidden mood straight away / it makes the reader curious about what is down there.

items.q: Find an expanded noun phrase in the third sentence. [1]
items.a: the heavy iron door (or: a cold breath of air)

items.q: Copy the main clause from the third sentence. [1]
items.a: a cold breath of air rushed past him

items.q: Find the relative clause in the second sentence and say what it tells us. [2]
items.a: 'which were covered in faded maps'. It gives extra information about the walls of the room (that they were covered in old maps), which adds detail to the description.

items.q: Why does the writer end with the short sentence 'He froze.'? [1]
items.a: After the longer sentences, the very short sentence stops the reader suddenly, showing Ali's shock and fear and building suspense about what he has found.

items.q: Find a relative clause in the first sentence. [1]
items.a: that nobody remembered
